papers.title: An Information-Theoretic Analysis of Information Hiding in Semantic Communication
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34550v1

summary.one_liner: The paper builds an information-theoretic framework for hiding messages in semantic communication, extending the classical Moulin-O'Sullivan information hiding model to a two-layer semantic/syntactic structure and characterizing its capacity as a Stackelberg maximin game with bounds relative to the classical capacity.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to hide a secret message inside communication that is judged by its meaning rather than by its exact symbols. The authors extend an existing mathematical model of hiding to a two-layer setup, where meaning and symbols are linked by mappings, and they define the maximum hidable rate as the result of a two-player game in which the hider moves first. They report that semantic hiding is not always better than classical hiding, and that the results are checked with binary, ternary and Gaussian examples.
summary.why: As semantic communication is explored for future networks, it is useful to know whether hiding information at the meaning level offers any real advantage over hiding at the symbol level. The text suggests the answer is conditional, with bounds showing when semantic hiding can fall short of the classical rate; the wider practical relevance is not assessed in the text.
summary.background:
- Information hiding (steganography): embedding a secret message in a cover signal so that the change is hard to notice.
- Channel capacity: the maximum rate at which information can be reliably sent, in bits per use of a channel.
- Mutual information: a measure of how much knowing one signal tells you about another.
- Semantic communication: transmitting the meaning of a message rather than exact symbols; synonymous mappings are many-to-one rewrites that preserve meaning.
- Stackelberg game: a two-player game where one player commits to a strategy first and the other responds.
- Maximin: choosing the strategy that maximizes the worst-case payoff.
- Random coding and joint typicality: standard proof techniques showing achievable rates and converse limits.

papers.abstract: Semantic communication shifts the transmission goal from the accurate recovery of syntactic symbols to the reliable conveyance of semantic content, yet a systematic information-theoretic characterization of information hiding at the semantic layer is still missing. Building on the semantic information theory of Niu-Zhang and the classical information hiding theory of Moulin-O'Sullivan, this paper establishes an information-theoretic framework for information hiding under semantic communication. The classical hiding model is extended to a two-layer structure (semantic host, syntactic host, syntactic composite signal, syntactic received, semantic received) bridged by synonymous mappings f_s, f_x and the inverse mapping f_y^{-1}, subject to four distortion constraints: syntactic transparency, semantic fidelity, syntactic perturbation, and semantic destruction. The capacity is cast as a Stackelberg game with the hider moving first and the payoff J(Q,A) = I(U~; Y~ | K) - I(U~; S~ | K), yielding the single-letter maximin C^s = max_Q min_A J(Q,A), whose achievability and converse follow from random coding and joint typicality decoding. Relative to the classical capacity, comparison payoffs built from the up/down semantic mutual information give the endpoint sandwich C^s_end(0,1) <= C^s <= C^s_end(1,0) with the classical value C in the same interval, while closing semantic tolerance yields C^s_no-tol <= C_cl under a fair comparison. These results clarify that semantic hiding is not unconditionally superior to classical hiding. Binary, ternary, and Gaussian examples confirm the degeneration under one-to-one mappings and the capacity loss under coarsening.

papers.title: Sharp one-shot bounds and optimal exponents of universal randomness extraction
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33270v1

summary.one_liner: The paper derives sharp one-shot bounds and optimal error exponents for quantum privacy amplification (randomness extraction against quantum side information) under universal hash families, via quadratically constrained hypothesis testing and connections to non-commutative Khintchine inequalities.
summary.plain:
The paper studies how to turn a partly leaked, imperfect source of random bits into nearly perfect secret randomness, when an eavesdropper may hold quantum information about it. It uses a method that reduces this to a family of statistical testing problems, and it pins down how fast the error shrinks in several regimes. The main claimed results are that a previously known bound is tight up to a constant factor for certain hash functions, and that the exact best error exponents are established for the asymptotic and strong converse settings.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Privacy amplification underlies quantum key distribution and secure randomness generation, so knowing the exact achievable error rates matters for those applications. The text does not show direct practical consequences, and the link to operator space theory is presented as a technical connection rather than a new application.
summary.background:
- Randomness extraction: converting a weak random source into nearly uniform, secret bits using a hash function.
- Quantum side information: an eavesdropper may hold quantum-correlated information about the source.
- Trace distance: the standard measure of how far a quantum state is from an ideal one, used as the security criterion.
- Universal hash families: random families of hash functions for which a randomly chosen member works well on average, with k-universality as a strength condition (2-universal, strongly 4-universal).
- One-shot versus i.i.d. settings: one-shot means a single use of the source; i.i.d. means many independent copies, where error decays exponentially at an exponent.
- Strong converse regime: the rate is above the limit, so success probability decays exponentially; the strong converse exponent measures that decay.
- Leftover hash lemma: a standard bound guaranteeing extraction quality; here it is being shown tight.
- Smooth entropy and hypothesis testing: information measures defined via allowed small perturbations and error trade-offs in distinguishing states.

papers.abstract: We introduce techniques for the study of randomness extraction against quantum side information (privacy amplification) by relating this problem to variants of hypothesis testing tasks with quadratic constraints. Building also on the recently introduced measured smooth entropy approach of [Regula and Tomamichel, arXiv:2603.04493], we precisely determine the optimal scaling of the error of quantum privacy amplification in several regimes. Our results apply to the standard operational security criterion based on trace distance and focus in particular on universal classes of hash functions. On the technical side, our investigation reveals connections with operator space theory methods used in non-commutative Khintchine inequalities. As one application, we give a one-shot converse bound that shows the leftover hash lemma of [arXiv:2603.04493] to be tight up to a constant factor for all strongly 4-universal hash functions. This allows us to evaluate the asymptotic i.i.d. error exponent of universal randomness extraction for all rates, matching the bound of [Dupuis, arXiv:2105.05342] and improving also earlier classical asymptotic results of [Hayashi, arXiv:1010.1358]. We furthermore give new one-shot achievability and converse bounds on the error in the strong converse regime, which we show to match up to a constant factor. This establishes the exact strong converse exponent of quantum privacy amplification under 2-universal hash functions, complementing the converse bound of [Shen, Gao, and Cheng, arXiv:2202.10263].

papers.title: Exponential Analysis for Trace-Distance Errors in Quantum Information Theory
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34468v1

summary.background:
- Quantum states: descriptions of quantum systems, often mixed, written as density matrices.
- Trace distance: a measure of how distinguishable two quantum states are, between 0 and 1.
- Reliability function: the exponent describing how quickly the error probability falls as the block length grows.
- Strong converse exponent: the exponent describing how quickly success vanishes when the transmission rate is pushed past the limit.
- Soft covering and convex splitting: protocols that make a random set of states look like a target state.
- Privacy amplification: shrinking a partly secret key so an eavesdropper who has quantum side information learns almost nothing.
- Decoupling: randomising a system so that it becomes uncorrelated with a part of itself or with a reference.
- Sandwiched and Petz Rényi information: families of entropy-like quantities that generalise Shannon information to quantum states.
- Quantum hypothesis testing: deciding which of two quantum states a system is in, the tool linking these errors to the exponents.
summary.one_liner: The paper determines exact exponential rates (reliability functions and strong converse exponents, in the i.i.d. setting) at which trace-distance errors vanish or blow up for classical-quantum soft covering, privacy amplification, convex splitting, and Haar-random decoupling, with formulas in terms of sandwiched and Petz Rényi information.
summary.plain: This paper is about how fast the error shrinks when quantum information is scrambled, shared, or hidden. The errors are measured with "trace distance," a standard way of asking how easily two quantum states can be told apart. The authors work out the exact exponential rates at which these errors fall (and, in the other regime, rise) for several standard quantum protocols when many copies are used.
summary.why: Exact error exponents tell engineers and theorists precisely how many resources a protocol needs for a given reliability, which matters for secure communication and quantum data processing. The text does not say how these results will be used in practice, so their wider impact is unclear from this summary alone.

papers.abstract: We study the trace-distance error in classical-quantum soft covering, privacy amplification against quantum side information, convex splitting, and decoupling by a Haar-random unitary followed by partial trace. In the independent and identically distributed setting, we determine exact reliability functions and strong converse exponents for soft covering with independent codewords, uniform convex splitting, and Haar partial-trace decoupling. For privacy amplification, we determine the exact reliability function for independent random binning and the exact strong converse exponent for every two-universal hash ensemble. The reliability and strong converse formulas involve sandwiched and Petz-R\'enyi information, respectively. The proofs connect trace-distance errors to quantum hypothesis testing, using Rosenthal inequalities for sums of random matrices in the reliability analysis and conditional second-moment bounds for the strong converses.

papers.title: What Must LLM Agents Communicate? From Information Loss to Communication Failures
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33318v1

summary.background:
- Multi-agent LLM system: several language-model instances that each see part of a problem and exchange messages.
- Information theory: the mathematical study of how much information can be stored, sent, and lost.
- Communication complexity: a field asking how many bits two or more parties must exchange to compute a joint answer.
- Sufficiency: whether a message keeps all the information needed for the final decision.
- Information loss: information discarded when an agent compresses its evidence into a summary, such as a probability report.
- Query-first interaction: an agent first states what it needs to know, so others send only relevant evidence.
summary.one_liner: A framework drawing on information theory and communication complexity that asks what messages LLM agents must exchange so a team can make accurate joint predictions when evidence is spread across them, tested with controlled experiments and message-level analysis.
summary.plain: Several AI agents may each hold a piece of the evidence needed for a decision, and together they may have enough to decide well, yet still fail to do so. The paper asks what those agents must tell each other, and when talking back and forth actually helps. The authors compare theoretical limits on how much information gets lost with the results of controlled experiments.
summary.why: Multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly used for joint reasoning, so knowing whether failures come from fundamental limits or from poor communication habits matters for designing them. The link to communication complexity and information loss gives the work a principled footing, though the text alone does not show how broadly the findings generalize beyond the authors' experiments.

papers.abstract: When evidence is distributed across LLM agents, a team may collectively possess all the information needed for a decision yet fail to use it effectively. What must agents communicate for accurate joint predictions, and when does interaction help? We study three requirements for effective communication: sufficiency of the information conveyed, selection of relevant evidence, and utilization of received information. Drawing on information theory and communication complexity, we develop a framework that combines theoretical benchmarks with controlled experiments and message-level analyses. We find that local probability reports can discard essential information, with theoretical information loss closely matching observed performance penalties. Query-first interaction improves predictions when relevant evidence depends on a private query, but compact one-shot representations can eliminate this advantage. Even when sufficient information is communicated, agents may fail to select or use it correctly. Together, these findings distinguish fundamental communication limits from failures in how LLM agents communicate and use information.

papers.title: Multi-User Linear Precoder Optimization for Obfuscation-Aided Mixed Regular and Wiretap Coding
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31840v1

summary.background:
- Wiretap coding: a way to send data so an eavesdropper learns almost nothing, relying on the receiver having a better channel.
- Regular (ordinary) channel coding: standard error-correction that maximizes data rate without secrecy.
- Secrecy rate: the amount of data per use of the channel that stays hidden from the eavesdropper.
- Obfuscation: scrambling the data with a secret key so it is unreadable without that key.
- Linear precoding: the transmitter weights signals across multiple antennas to aim beams at chosen users.
- Beampattern: a map of how signal strength varies with direction, used to see where a transmitter sends energy.
- Line-of-sight (LoS) channel: a channel dominated by a direct path between transmitter and receiver, modeled from geometry.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a generalized obfuscation-aided mixed wiretap/regular coding system built on multi-user linear precoding, formulates the precoder optimization with a minimum secrecy rate constraint, and studies it with simulations on a geometric two-user line-of-sight channel.
summary.plain: Wireless signals can be overheard by an eavesdropper, and a common defense is "wiretap coding," which hides data by exploiting the fact that the intended receiver has a better channel than the eavesdropper. When that advantage is small, this defense sharply cuts how much data can be sent. This paper studies a mixed scheme: a short secret is protected with wiretap coding, and that secret is used to scramble the main data, which is then sent with ordinary error-correcting code. The authors design how the transmitter aims its signals for two users and report simulation results on how the scheme behaves.
summary.why: It addresses a practical limit of physical-layer security, where secrecy is provided by the channel itself rather than by encryption, and it may matter for future wireless systems. The text reports simulation results only, so its practical significance beyond the modeled geometric channel is not established.

papers.abstract: Physical-layer security has attracted considerable research interest with the development of quantum computing. One prominent approach is wiretap coding, which exploits the channel advantage of a legitimate receiver over an eavesdropper to achieve secure communication. However, under unfavorable channel conditions, wiretap coding can significantly reduce the achievable rate compared to regular channel coding. Mixed coding alleviates this limitation by using wiretap coding to protect a short secret required for obfuscation, while the obfuscated payload is encoded using regular channel coding. In this work, we propose a generalized obfuscation-aided mixed-coding system based on the multi-user (MU)-linear precoding (LP) architecture that unifies existing approaches employing different obfuscation functions. We then formulate the corresponding precoder optimization problem, abstracting the obfuscation function through a minimum secrecy rate constraint. Numerical simulations using a geometric two-user line-of-sight (LoS) channel demonstrated how the minimum secrecy rate requirement determines the operating point of mixed coding between regular and wiretap coding. Subsequent beampattern analysis revealed a key synergy between mixed coding and precoding: Mixed coding enables individual beam shaping for the two coding layers. Finally, spatial analysis showed that mixed coding offers the largest sum-rate gains when users are positioned at similar angles.

papers.title: Self-Orthogonal Minimal Codes from n-to-1 Mappings
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32192v1

summary.background:
- Linear code: a set of vectors over a finite field (a number system with finitely many elements) closed under addition and scaling; its weight is the count of nonzero entries in a codeword.
- Weight distribution: how many codewords have each possible weight; it reveals a code's error-correcting behaviour.
- Self-orthogonal code: a code whose codewords are orthogonal to one another, a property needed for quantum error-correcting codes.
- Minimal code: a code where no codeword's support is contained in another's; this lets its supports define access rules for secret sharing.
- n-to-1 mapping: a function where exactly n inputs share each output value; Walsh spectrum and linearized polynomials are standard tools for analysing such functions.
- Skew polynomial ring: a generalisation of ordinary polynomials in which variables do not commute, with a "right greatest common divisor" used as the key computational tool.
summary.one_liner: Using right greatest common divisors of skew polynomials to find kernel dimensions of linearized polynomials, the paper derives exact weight distributions and proves minimality and self-orthogonality for linear codes from three families of n-to-1 mappings over finite fields.
summary.plain: This paper is about error-correcting codes, the mathematical recipes used to protect data from corruption. It studies codes built from certain functions that map many inputs to one output, and it is hard to count how often their codewords have each weight for complicated functions. The authors use an algebraic tool called skew polynomial rings to work out those counts for two new function families and one known family, and they show the resulting codes have two useful properties.
summary.why: The codes are claimed to be both self-orthogonal, which is the property used in building quantum error-correcting codes, and minimal, which is the property used in secret-sharing schemes, so one family could serve both purposes. The text does not say how these codes would perform in practice, so the practical significance is unclear from this text alone.

papers.abstract: Self-orthogonal codes are central to the construction of quantum error-correcting codes, and minimal codes yield secret-sharing schemes whose access structures are read off from the supports of their codewords. A code that is both self-orthogonal and minimal therefore serves both purposes at once, so that a single family of codes can produce a quantum code and a secret-sharing scheme simultaneously. Linear codes arising from n-to-1 mappings over finite fields are a natural source of such codes and have attracted considerable attention recently, yet their parameters and weight distributions remain difficult to determine: for most high-degree functions the Walsh spectra cannot be computed directly, and it is precisely these weights on which the analysis of minimality and self-orthogonality rests. We address this difficulty through the algebraic theory of skew polynomial rings. Using the right greatest common divisor of skew polynomials, we determine the dimensions of the kernel spaces of the linearized polynomials associated with the n-to-1 mappings, which in turn yield the weight distributions of the corresponding codes. With this method we treat two newly constructed families of n-to-1 functions together with one known family, and obtain the exact weight distributions of the resulting codes; we further prove that all of these codes are minimal and self-orthogonal. Each family therefore simultaneously yields a quantum error-correcting code and a secret-sharing scheme, with explicitly determined parameters and access structures. This work offers a new perspective for determining the parameters of linear codes derived from n-to-1 mappings.

papers.title: Optimal fidelity over zero-capacity erasure channels
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30902v1

summary.background:
- Quantum channel: a physical process that sends quantum states (such as qubits) from sender to receiver, possibly adding noise.
- Erasure channel: a noise model where each transmitted piece either arrives intact (with probability γ) or is lost and flagged as missing.
- Channel capacity: the maximum rate at which reliable communication is possible; zero capacity means no reliable communication.
- Antidegradable channel: a channel where the environment can obtain at least as much information as the receiver, so the receiver cannot get reliable quantum information.
- Entanglement fidelity: a score from 0 to 1 measuring how well entanglement with a reference system is preserved; the formula γ + (1−γ)/d is the value found here, where d is the dimension of the logical message.
- Fractional extendibility: a mathematical tool used to derive the upper bound on achievable fidelity.
- Asymptotic: referring to the limit of long block lengths.
summary.one_liner: The paper exactly finds the optimal asymptotic entanglement fidelity of quantum erasure channels in the antidegradable regime (transmission probability at most 1/2), matching an upper bound from fractional extendibility with a permutation-invariant code family.
summary.plain: The paper asks how well a quantum message can survive a noisy channel that is too noisy to carry any reliable information at all, yet still preserves some of it. For a common noise model, where each piece of the message is either passed through or lost, the authors work out the best achievable fidelity (how closely the received quantum state matches the original). They find it equals a simple formula, and they show that codes can reach this value.
summary.why: It gives a precise answer to a question about what is possible in the regime where reliable quantum communication is impossible, which is a useful boundary for the theory. The text does not say how widely the result applies beyond erasure channels, so its broader significance is uncertain.

papers.abstract: Antidegradable quantum channels have zero capacity for reliable quantum communication. However, they can nevertheless transmit quantum information with nontrivial fidelity. This raises the question: how well can quantum information be preserved through such channels? In this work, we exactly characterize the optimal asymptotic entanglement fidelity of quantum erasure channels throughout the antidegradable regime. Specifically, we show that it equals $\gamma+\frac{1-\gamma}{d}$ for transmission probabilities $0<\gamma\le \frac{1}{2}$ and logical dimension $d$. We use fractional extendibility to establish an upper bound on the entanglement fidelity achievable by arbitrary error-correcting protocols. Furthermore, we construct a family of permutation-invariant codes that asymptotically saturates this bound.

papers.title: Super-Multiplicativity of the Noncommutative Minimum and Applications to Quantum Privacy and Hypothesis Testing
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30038v1

summary.background:
- Quantum states: mathematical descriptions of quantum systems, represented by positive semidefinite operators (matrices) with trace.
- Trace and trace norm: sum of diagonal entries; the trace norm measures how different two operators are.
- Hockey-stick divergence: a measure of distinguishability between two states, tied to differential privacy guarantees.
- Differential privacy: a guarantee that outputs barely change when one input record is swapped for a neighboring one.
- Binary hypothesis testing: deciding which of two states a system is in, given copies of it; error probabilities are the key quantity.
- Chernoff bound: the exponential rate at which the error probability of such tests decays with the number of copies; the paper finds its exact prefactor (the constant multiplying the exponential).
- Sub-additivity and super-multiplicativity: inequalities relating a quantity on combined systems to the same quantity on each part.
- Commuting vs. noncommuting states: classical (commuting) states behave like ordinary probability distributions; quantum (noncommuting) ones do not, which makes the analysis harder.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves that a noncommutative generalization of the minimum of two positive operators is super-multiplicative, and uses this to derive sub-additivity bounds for the quantum hockey-stick divergence on product states, with applications to quantum differential privacy and symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing (including the exact Chernoff prefactor).
summary.plain: The paper studies how well two quantum states can be told apart when they are combined from separate parts, using a standard measure called the hockey-stick divergence. The authors prove an inequality for a quantity they call the noncommutative minimum, and show it implies that the divergence for combined systems is bounded in a clean way. They then apply this to privacy guarantees for quantum channels and to the error rate of distinguishing two quantum states from many copies.
summary.why: Quantum differential privacy and quantum hypothesis testing both rely on this divergence, so bounds on how it behaves for combined systems matter for how privacy budgets compose and how fast errors shrink with more samples. The text states the bounds are tight and that the Chernoff prefactor and sample-complexity result hold under stated conditions; its practical impact beyond these theory settings is not discussed in the text.

papers.abstract: The hockey-stick divergence is a fundamental distinguishability measure in quantum information theory. It characterizes quantum differential privacy and determines the optimal error probability of binary quantum hypothesis testing with arbitrary priors. We study how it behaves on tensor-product states. To this end, we consider the noncommutative minimum $m(A,B):=(\mathrm{Tr}[A]+\mathrm{Tr}[B]-\|A-B\|_1)/2$ of positive semidefinite operators, which reduces to $\sum_x\min\{a_x,b_x\}$ when $A$ and $B$ commute, and we prove that it is super-multiplicative, i.e., $m(A\otimes C,B\otimes D)\ge m(A,B)\,m(C,D)$. As a consequence, we establish a sub-additivity property of the hockey-stick divergence on product states, in which the parameters of the individual systems are multiplied, and no additional prefactor appears. We show that this bound is tight, also for noncommuting states, and that it is strict for faithful states whenever at least two of the divergences are positive. Using this, we obtain sub-additivity of the Datta-Leditzky divergences, a parallel composition theorem for quantum differentially private channels under product neighboring inputs with at most linear degradation of the privacy parameters, and a sharp sub-additivity property of the hypothesis-testing relative entropy normalized by the acceptance probability. Finally, we apply the same tools to symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing. We determine the exact prefactor of the quantum Chernoff bound for every pair of noncommuting states satisfying mild conditions including a nonlattice condition and, under a quantitative version of this condition, the full asymptotic expansion to every fixed order in $1/n$, with explicitly computable coefficients. As a consequence, we determine the sample complexity of symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing up to one sample, as the error probability tends to zero.

papers.title: Coding Length and Optimal Power Allocation in Correlated Block Fading
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27694v1

summary.background:
- Block fading: the channel gain stays fixed within a block and changes between blocks.
- Outage: the event that the channel is too weak to support a chosen rate; outage probability is its chance.
- Error exponent: how fast the chance of decoding error shrinks as a parameter (here, the number of receive antennas) grows.
- Dispersion: a measure of how much the achievable rate fluctuates around the capacity for finite-length codes.
- Power allocation: how a fixed total energy is split across the blocks of a codeword.
- Autoregressive (AR(1)) fading: a model where each block's gain is correlated with the previous one.
summary.one_liner: For a Gaussian block-fading channel with correlated fades, the paper studies when outage probability predicts the achievable rate under an exponential error-exponent requirement with many receive antennas, and it characterizes the optimal power allocation across blocks.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how to send a message reliably over a wireless link where signal strength varies in blocks of time that are correlated with each other. The transmitter knows only the statistical pattern of the fading, not the actual values, and the receiver has many antennas. The authors find when the simple "outage" measure (the chance the link is too weak to support a rate) correctly predicts the best rate, and when it overestimates it.
summary.why: It sharpens when a standard engineering shortcut for wireless links, outage, is accurate, and it gives explicit examples where power should be left off a block and then used again as reliability demands tighten. The text does not indicate links to specific applications beyond wireless communication.

papers.abstract: A codeword spans a fixed number of correlated Gaussian fading blocks. The receiver knows the gains and the transmitter knows only their law. At fixed average signal-to-noise ratio, we require the decoding error probability to decay exponentially with the number of receive antennas. When does outage predict the achievable rate? If block length grows faster than the number of antennas, outage gives the limiting optimal rate. If both grow to infinity at a fixed positive ratio of block length to array size, outage strictly overestimates the limiting rate. We determine the critical ratio above which positive rates are possible. For sufficiently large finite ratios, we find the exact limiting rate over all codes satisfying a total energy constraint on each codeword. The leading rate loss is inversely proportional to the ratio. Its coefficient depends on Gaussian channel dispersion at the most likely fade causing outage and on how quickly the outage rate decreases as the required error exponent increases. In the long-block limit, equal power loses rate on every window of three or more blocks under stationary first-order autoregressive fading with positive lag-one correlation. In a different three-block channel with identical marginal gains, tightening the reliability requirement first makes it optimal to leave the middle block unused and later to use it again.

papers.title: $L^1$ stability of the entropy power inequality in $\mathbb{R}^d$ without moment assumptions
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27790v1

summary.background:
- Differential entropy: a measure of spread or uncertainty for a continuous random vector, with a density function.
- Entropy power inequality: a bound saying the entropy power of a sum of independent random vectors is at least the sum of their entropy powers; equality holds for Gaussians.
- Stability: if the inequality is almost an equality, the distributions are close to Gaussian-type extremizers in some measured distance.
- L^1 distance: the total amount by which two probability densities differ, integrated over space.
- Ruzsa distance: a distance between random variables that is used in additive combinatorics and probability.
- Optimal transport: a way of moving one probability distribution into another at minimal cost, used here as a proof tool.
- Young's inequality: a sharp inequality on convolutions of functions; its sharp form has known extremizers (Gaussians).
- Moment assumptions: conditions that random variables have finite averages of powers of their size; the paper removes these.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves qualitative stability of Shannon's entropy power inequality in R^d in L^1 and Ruzsa distance without any moment assumptions, using an optimal transport argument, majorization of density rearrangements, and Christ's stability result for sharp Young's inequality.
summary.plain:
The paper studies a basic inequality from information theory that bounds how the uncertainty (entropy) of a sum of independent random quantities relates to that of the parts. It asks what happens when that inequality is nearly tight, and shows the near-equality stays close in a precise sense, without requiring the random quantities to have finite moments (a technical condition on how spread out they can be). The authors also extend several earlier one-dimensional results to random vectors of any dimension.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Stability results say that near-optimal cases must look close to the extremal ones, which matters for proofs and for understanding when the bound is sharp. The text does not describe applications beyond this mathematical setting, so any wider connections are unclear from the abstract alone.

papers.abstract: We establish qualitative stability in $L^1$ and Ruzsa distance for Shannon's entropy power inequality in $\mathbb{R}^d$, without any moment assumptions. The proof uses the optimal transport argument by Rioul (2017), majorization bounds of density rearrangements, and the stability of the sharp form of Young's inequality due to Christ (2019). Along the way we also extend recent one-dimensional results on de Bruijn's identity, the continuity of differential entropy, and the equality case of the entropy power inequality to random vectors of any dimension.

papers.title: Optimal Impure $(r,δ)$-Quantum Locally Recoverable Codes with Explicit Minimum Localities
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25859v1

summary.background:
- Error-correcting codes: adding redundancy so that erased or corrupted symbols can be recovered.
- Erasure and qudit: a qudit is a quantum unit with d levels (a generalization of a qubit); an erasure is a known loss of such a unit.
- Locality (r, δ): any δ−1 erased units can be recovered by reading only r others; the minimum locality is the smallest such r.
- Recovering sets: groups of units that can be used together to repair a loss; disjoint sets mean the groups do not overlap.
- CSS codes: a construction of quantum codes built from two classical linear codes, here a nested pair C and its relative.
- Singleton-like bound: a theoretical upper limit on how good a code can be; GKT-optimal means a code meets this limit.
- Monomial-Cartesian codes: algebraic evaluation codes built from polynomial monomials on a grid.
summary.one_liner: The paper builds quantum locally recoverable codes with disjoint recovering sets from nested generalized monomial-Cartesian CSS code pairs, obtaining four infinite families that are optimal under the GKT Singleton-like bound and determining their minimum localities.
summary.plain: This paper is about quantum error-correcting codes, which protect quantum information by spreading it across many storage units (qudits) so that lost units can be rebuilt. The authors design a family of such codes where a missing unit can be restored by reading only a small number r of other units, with the goal of recovering as many lost units as possible at once. They report four infinite families of codes that meet a known theoretical limit (the GKT bound) and work out, for each allowed level of protection, the smallest such r and which units to read.
summary.why: Locality, meaning how few other units must be read to repair a loss, matters for storage and distributed systems where reading data is costly, and the paper gives exact answers rather than only bounds. The text does not indicate applications beyond coding theory, so the practical reach is unclear from the abstract alone.

papers.abstract: Quantum locally recoverable codes with $(r,δ)$-locality ($(r,δ)$-qLRCs) are quantum error-correcting codes in which $δ-1$ erased qudits can be recovered by accessing only $r$ other qudits. The minimum locality of a qLRC is the least $r$ such that it has $(r,δ)$-locality. This paper aims to construct optimal impure $(r,δ)$-qLRCs with disjoint recovering sets and explicit minimum localities, where the optimality is measured by the Singleton-like bound of Guruswami, Kshirsagar, and Trivedi (GKT-optimal). Such qLRCs have particular advantages in recovering as many quantum erasures as possible while operating in parallel and with minimal qudit access overhead. We first characterize the recovering sets and the minimum locality of any CSS code by local relative distances, which are relative minimum distances of punctured codes with respect to shortened codes. We then construct impure qLRCs as CSS codes from nested pairs of generalized monomial-Cartesian codes. Grouping the monomials by their degree in the last variable, we reduce both their minimum distances and their local recovery to nested pairs of codes in the remaining variables, and the coordinates with the same values of these variables form disjoint recovering sets. In this way, we obtain four infinite families of GKT-optimal impure $(r,δ)$-qLRCs with disjoint recovering sets, and determine their minimum localities and the recovering sets attaining them for every admissible $δ$, except for a partial range of $δ$ in one family. These minimum localities need not be monotone in $δ$. In particular, two of the families contain GKT-optimal impure subfamilies of CSS codes CSS$(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C})$ with $(r,δ)$-locality for some $r<n-δ+1$ at values of $δ$ for which $\mathcal{C}$ has no classical $(r',δ)$-locality for any $0<r'<n$, where $n$ is the length of $\mathcal{C}$.

papers.title: Convex splitting by binary quantum hypothesis testing
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25496v1

summary.background:
- Quantum state: a mathematical description of a quantum system, written as a density operator.
- Reference system: a second system whose correlation with the hidden system is what the observer tries to detect.
- Trace distance: a measure of how distinguishable two quantum states are (0 means identical, 1 means perfectly distinguishable).
- Convex split lemma: a statement that a mixture of correlated states can be made close to a product of independent copies, given enough copies.
- Binary hypothesis testing: deciding between two possible states using one measurement with two outcomes; relative entropy here measures how hard this is.
- Secret key distillation: turning correlated, partly eavesdropped randomness into shared secret bits.
- Asymptotic repetitions and log terms: results for n independent uses, where the leftover loss grows like log n.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves one-shot quantum convex-split bounds via binary hypothesis testing, and applies them to private communication, one-way secret key distillation, and a position-based key protocol with a log n loss term.
summary.plain: The paper asks how many separate quantum systems are needed to hide one system that is linked to a reference system, so that an observer measuring all of them cannot tell the hidden one apart from an unrelated pair. The authors turn this into a set of simple yes-or-no tests and derive bounds on how many systems suffice. They then use these bounds to estimate how many secret bits can be sent or shared, including what an eavesdropper might learn publicly.
summary.why: The results give explicit one-shot bounds for private communication and key distillation, which connects quantum information theory to practical secret-key questions. The text does not show how these bounds compare with other methods in practice, so their practical reach is unclear.

papers.abstract: How many independent quantum systems does it take to hide one system that is correlated with a reference? An observer can measure all the systems together with the reference to detect the correlation. We turn any such measurement into binary tests on a single system and the reference. For each test we bound the probability of declaring a signal when an independent pair was prepared. Averaging the largest signal acceptance probabilities allowed by these bounds controls the normalized trace distance in the convex-split lemma. A second bound gives a sufficient number of systems by minimizing the hypothesis-testing relative entropy over the state of the reference. Both bounds hold for density operators on separable Hilbert spaces. Comparing two distributions for the location of the hidden system gives one-shot bounds for private communication and one-way secret key distillation, including the public information available to an eavesdropper. For a fixed finite-alphabet model with separable quantum outputs and positive information advantage and variances, we recover the known Gaussian corrections to the attainable number of private or key bits from $n$ independent repetitions and bound the remaining loss by $\log_2 n+O(1)$ at fixed errors. The position-based key distillation protocol attains this bound with $O(n)$ public bits.

papers.title: Benchmarking Traditional and Learning-Based Reference-Free Compressors for Long-Read Sequencing Data
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23794v1

summary.one_liner: A benchmark and survey of 35 reference-free lossless compressors (traditional and learning-based) evaluated on 16 real Oxford Nanopore and PacBio long-read sequencing datasets, comparing compression ratio, runtime, memory, and robustness.
summary.plain:
Modern DNA sequencing machines produce very large files, which are costly to store and send. This paper tests many software tools that shrink these files without needing a reference genome (a standard DNA text to compare against). The authors ran 35 such tools on 16 real datasets and compared how much they shrink the data, how fast they run, how much memory they use, and how consistent they are.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Storage and transfer costs are a practical bottleneck for long-read sequencing, so knowing which tools work best without a reference is useful to labs. The text reports that CoLoRd gave the best overall compression in these tests, but the results only cover the datasets and settings the authors used.</plain>
<parameter name="background">- Lossless compression: shrinking a file so it can be restored exactly, bit for bit.
- Compression ratio: original size divided by compressed size; higher means smaller output.
- Long-read sequencing: technology (Oxford Nanopore, PacBio) that reads DNA in long pieces, producing large files.
- Reference-based vs reference-free: reference-based tools compress by comparing to a known genome; reference-free tools do not need one, which matters when no suitable genome exists.
- Learning-based compressors: tools that use machine-learning models to predict the data, usually slower and more costly to run.
- Multithreading: running parts of a program on several processor cores at once to speed it up.

papers.abstract: Long-read sequencing technologies generate large volumes of data, creating substantial storage and transmission demands. Although reference-based compressors can achieve high compression, their reliance on an appropriate reference genome limits their use. We present LRCBench, a benchmark and survey of reference-free lossless compressors for long-read sequencing data. We review traditional and learning-based general-purpose and sequencing-specific methods, then evaluate 35 compressors on 16 real-world datasets from Oxford Nanopore and PacBio platforms. We compare compression ratio, storage savings, runtime, peak memory use, and robustness across datasets. Learning-based compressors are evaluated on six MinION datasets because of their high computational costs. CoLoRd achieves the best overall compression ratios in our experiments, while other methods offer trade-offs in speed, memory use, and robustness. We also examine multithreaded speedup and discuss future directions in parallel acceleration, privacy protection, adaptive parameter tuning, and hardware-algorithm co-design.

papers.title: Learning Integer Winding Evolution Times in Quantum Phase Estimation
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25124v1

summary.background:
- Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE): a quantum algorithm that reads out an eigenvalue (energy level) of an operator as a phase angle.
- Hamiltonian: the operator describing a system's energy; evolving under it for a time t imprints phases tied to energies.
- Eigenvalue / minimum eigenvalue: the lowest energy level, often the target of ground-state calculations.
- Qubits and digitization error: the phase is stored in a finite number of binary digits, so precision is limited by the number of qubits.
- Shannon entropy: a measure of spread or uncertainty in a probability distribution; low entropy means outcomes cluster tightly.
- Quantum magnet models: standard test systems (spin lattices) used to benchmark quantum algorithms.
- Near-term quantum computing: work targeting current noisy hardware where shallow circuits are needed.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes learning the Hamiltonian evolution time in Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) by minimizing the Shannon entropy of the measured phase distribution, reporting improved minimum-eigenvalue accuracy on quantum magnet models.
summary.plain: Quantum Phase Estimation is a quantum-computing procedure for finding the lowest energy of a physical system, and its accuracy is normally limited by how finely the answer can be encoded in qubits. This paper adds an optimization loop that tunes the evolution time so the measured results are less spread out (lower Shannon entropy, a measure of how unpredictable a set of outcomes is). The authors report that this improves the estimate of the minimum energy in numerical tests on quantum magnet models.
summary.why: If the approach holds up, it could make QPE useful on near-term quantum hardware by allowing shorter, shallower circuits for physics problems. The text gives only a brief summary and numerical tests on magnet models, so its broader significance and how it compares with other methods are not established here.

papers.abstract: Learning a Hamiltonian evolution time in Quantum Phase Estimation that produces phase distributions with low Shannon entropy circumvents the fundamental limit of digitization error of phase, independent of the number of phase qubits of accuracy. By introducing an optimization loop to minimize the Shannon entropy of measured eigenvalues produced by a QPE quantum circuit, minimum eigenvalue computation accuracy is greatly improved, which we show numerically on quantum magnet models. This technique works because standard QPE has a natural correspondence between entropy of the phase distribution and the analog accuracy of the minimum eigenvalue phase. This introduces for the first time a type of parameter learning to QPE, which makes near term practicality of QPE for fundamental sciences more feasible by using shorter depth QPE circuits.

papers.title: blaris: Windowless Random-Access LZSS for Constrained Microcontrollers
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22900v1

summary.background:
- Compression: shrinking data by replacing repeated pieces with short references to earlier text.
- LZ77 / LZSS: a family of compression methods that refers back to earlier output; LZSS marks each piece as either a literal or a back-reference.
- Sliding window: the recent stretch of decoded data kept in RAM so back-references can be resolved; its size trades memory against compression.
- Microcontroller: a small, low-power chip with very little RAM and flash storage.
- Execute-in-place (XIP): running or reading code and data straight from flash without copying it into RAM first.
- Random access: reading a chosen piece of data without decoding everything before it.
- Checkpoints: stored markers that let a decoder jump to a known position in the stream.
- Trusted payload: the compressed data is made on a computer ahead of time and assumed valid, so the device skips error checks to save code.
summary.one_liner: blaris is a windowless LZSS decompressor for execute-in-place random access on RV32IMC microcontrollers, resolving back-references inside the compressed payload using bidirectional token streams with power-of-two checkpoints.
summary.plain: Tiny microcontroller chips often store data compressed to save space, but the usual decompression methods need a chunk of working memory that grows with how well the data is squeezed, and reading a small piece from the middle is slow. This paper presents blaris, a decompressor designed to avoid that working memory and to read small pieces of compressed data directly from flash storage. The authors report it fits in roughly 548 to 784 bytes of flash and 104 to 112 bytes of RAM on a RISC-V chip, and that small random reads are far faster than block-indexed versions of two existing decompressors at similar compression ratios.
summary.why: Memory is the main limit on very small devices, so a decompressor that needs almost no RAM and still supports fast random reads could matter for firmware and embedded data storage. The text gives benchmark figures but not the full test setup, so the size of the advantage should be checked against the full paper.

papers.abstract: Embedded LZ77 decompressors (such as heatshrink and tamp) require an in-RAM sliding window that couples memory usage to compression ratio and incurs high latency on random-access reads. We present blaris, a lightweight, windowless LZSS decompressor for execute-in-place (XIP) random access on constrained microcontrollers. By partitioning tokens into bidirectionally traversable streams with power-of-two checkpoints, blaris resolves back-references directly in the compressed payload, achieving compression ratios comparable to high-window heatshrink and tamp configurations without allocating a RAM window. Targeting compress-on-host, decompress-on-device workflows, blaris assumes trusted build-time payloads and omits runtime error and bounds checks. On RV32IMC, it requires just 548-784 B of Flash and 104-112 B of total RAM, achieving orders-of-magnitude faster small-slice random reads than ratio-matched, block-indexed heatshrink and tamp.

papers.title: Electromagnetic Channel Model and Sensing Performance for ISAC: The Case of a Single Cylindrical Scatterer
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23503v1

summary.background:
- Channel model: a mathematical description of how a signal travels from transmitter to receiver, including reflections.
- ISAC (integrated sensing and communication): using one wireless system to both communicate and detect or locate objects.
- Scattering: how waves are redirected when they hit an object.
- Near field vs. far field: close to a source, where wave behavior is complex, versus far away, where it simplifies.
- Permittivity / dielectric constant: how strongly a material responds to an electric field, which affects how it reflects waves.
- Cramér-Rao lower bound: the best accuracy any unbiased estimator can achieve for a given measurement setup.
- 3GPP: the standards body that defines cellular network specifications, including channel models.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a physics-based, electromagnetic wireless channel model (an impedance channel transfer matrix from wave scattering theory with boundary conditions) for a single dielectric cylindrical target, valid in both near and far fields, and evaluates target localization accuracy via the Cramér-Rao lower bound for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC).
summary.plain: The paper builds a detailed physics model of how radio waves bounce off a single object, here idealized as a cylinder, so that a wireless system can work out where that object is. The model accounts for waves interacting with the object and with each other, and it is meant to work both close to the transmitter and far from it. The authors use it to estimate how precisely the object's position, size, and dielectric constant (how it responds to electric fields) could be measured, but the text does not report specific numerical results.
summary.why: Future wireless networks are expected to sense their surroundings as well as carry data, so channel models that capture real electromagnetic effects could matter for that work. The text also mentions possible extensions to extended targets and to 3GPP standard channel modeling, but how far this would carry into practical standards is not shown here.

papers.abstract: We propose an electromagnetic wireless channel model for accurate target localization in radar-like sensing scenarios. The model employs a self-consistent method grounded in wave scattering theory and imposing boundary conditions, providing the (impedance) channel transfer matrix for a propagation channel with a single target modeled as a cylindrical scatterer. The model is: 1) physics-based, as it includes electromagnetic interactions between objects; 2) unified, as it is valid in both near- and far-field regions. Within the canonical two-dimensional and 2.5-dimensional configurations with line-source and dipole-source excitations, respectively, the model supports dielectric cylinders with frequency-dependent permittivity. Localization accuracy is assessed via the Cramer-Rao lower bound for a dielectric cylinder with variable position, radius, and dielectric constant. Provisions for future extensions to extended targets are discussed in the context of 3GPP channel modeling.

papers.title: The Sample Complexity of Channel Coding
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21395v1

summary.background:
- Channel coding: encoding messages with redundancy so they can be recovered after noise corrupts them.
- Blocklength: the number of symbols in one coded message.
- Error probability: the chance the receiver decodes the wrong message.
- Channel capacity: the highest rate achievable with vanishing error for very long blocks (the asymptotic limit).
- Rényi-type capacities of order α: generalized information measures, parameterized by α; order 1/2 is the case discussed here.
- Cutoff rate: an older coding-theory benchmark for practical decoding effort.
- Hypothesis testing: deciding between two possible distributions from data; used here as a tool for proving limits.
- AWGN channel: a channel adding Gaussian noise, with a limit on transmit power.
summary.one_liner: Introduces a nonasymptotic "sample complexity" framework for channel coding, showing that for discrete memoryless channels the minimal blocklength is governed by the Augustin–Csiszár (equivalently cutoff rate and Sibson) capacity of order 1/2 rather than ordinary capacity, with a one-shot hypothesis-testing converse and explicit AWGN results.
summary.plain: This paper asks how long a message must be, in terms of the number of symbols sent, before a noisy communication channel can carry information reliably at a target rate and error level. Instead of the usual question of the best rate for very long messages, it studies the smallest workable block length directly, with explicit constants. The authors find that this length is set by a different quantity than the familiar channel capacity, namely a related measure of order 1/2 (the cutoff rate).
summary.why: The result shifts attention from asymptotic capacity to concrete finite-length behavior, which matters for practical codes with limited delay. The link to the cutoff rate, an older quantity from coding theory, is the notable connection, though the text alone does not show how practical this is for specific systems.

papers.abstract: We introduce a new framework for the study and evaluation of the fundamental limits of channel coding, emphasizing genuinely nonasymptotic results. The {\em channel coding sample complexity} $n^*({\cal W},ε)$ of a channel ${\cal W}$ is defined as the smallest blocklength at which it is possible to transmit information through that channel with error probability below $ε$ and at a rate at least as high as that given by an appropriate constraint also in terms of $ε$. This formulation follows analogous developments in statistics, computer science and, more recently, in lossless source coding. For any discrete memoryless channel we derive nonasymptotic bounds on the sample complexity, with explicit constants. These bounds show that the sample complexity is characterized not by the usual channel capacity, but by the channel's Augustin--Csiszár capacity of order $1/2$, which coincides with the cutoff rate as well as with the channel's Sibson capacity of order $1/2$. The proof is partly based on a new channel-coding one-shot converse in terms of hypothesis testing. We also examine extensions of the sample complexity framework to general target rates. Moreover, we derive corresponding results for the sample complexity of the additive white Gaussian noise channel with a quadratic power constraint. Their proof relies on new, explicit upper bounds on the best achievable error probability, which may be of independent interest.

papers.title: Neural Classifiers as Error-Correcting Codes
papers.label: arXiv:2611.18239v2

summary.background:
- Error-correcting codes: a way to add structured redundancy to a message so a receiver can recover it despite noise.
- Codeword: the fixed pattern assigned to each message or class.
- Hamming distance: the number of positions in which two patterns differ.
- Maximum-likelihood decoding: picking the codeword most likely to have produced what was received.
- Softmax and cross-entropy: the standard output scoring and training loss for classifiers.
- Neural Collapse: a late-training phenomenon where class representations form a symmetric, evenly spaced arrangement.
- Knowledge distillation: training a smaller network to copy a larger one's outputs.
- Self-supervised learning: training representations without labels.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes viewing supervised deep classifiers as Shannon-style error-correcting code decoders, claiming cross-entropy training aligns softmax outputs with maximum-likelihood decoding over class codewords, and extends this to Neural Collapse, LeJEPA and self-supervised encoders.
summary.plain: Neural networks that sort inputs into categories, such as recognizing images, are trained with a standard scoring rule. This paper argues that the same job can be seen as the problem of decoding a message sent through a noisy channel, where each category has a fixed codeword. From that view, the authors say the standard training rule, the shape of the learned representations, and some practical tools such as compression and distillation can be explained together.
summary.why: If the analogy holds, it could link deep learning training and representation geometry to a well-established body of coding theory, which may suggest new criteria for compression and regularization. The text itself gives only a high-level abstract, so how far the claims are supported by proofs or experiments cannot be judged from it; the authors' stated results should be checked in the full paper.

papers.abstract: A unified framework is proposed that characterizes supervised deep classification as the decoding of error-correcting codes in the Shannon sense. Cross-entropy optimization is shown to align softmax classifiers with maximum-likelihood decoding, where logits map to Hamming distances to class-specific codewords. This correspondence explains the emergence of standard divergence objectives (e.g., Kullback-Leibler, Jeffreys, Bregman) and provides a geometric basis for the stability of decision boundaries. Furthermore, the geometries of Neural Collapse and LeJEPA are identified as optimal constellations for decoding under isotropic noise. Unlike classical Error-Correcting Output Codes, deep networks are shown to learn effective codebooks in the feature space implicitly. This insight is leveraged to derive novel criteria for lossless quantization, improved knowledge distillation, and architectural regularization based on code redundancy. Finally, this perspective is extended to self-supervised encoders, offering a cohesive explanation for the geometry of latent representations in modern neural models.
